title: Your AI Is Doing Extra Work
notes:
- Hi, I’m Vijay. Thanks to the OpenAI Student Collective at Waterloo for co-sponsoring this talk.
- When a model runs, it spends time calculating, moving data and waiting for work to start. Today we’ll look at how a compiler can make that run faster.
- We’ll use a few small examples, so you can follow along without knowing much about GPUs or compilers.
takeaway: The same intended computation can have different execution costs.
transition: Let’s start with three numbers.

title: One computation, two execution plans
notes:
- We have negative five, one and four. This array of numbers is a tensor.
- We want to add three to each number and then apply ReLU. ReLU replaces negative values with zero and leaves the other values alone.
- [Start the animation with Space. Continue speaking as it runs.]
- After adding three, we have negative two, four and seven. Applying ReLU gives us zero, four and seven.
- In the first version, addition saves its answer in a temporary array. ReLU then reads that array to do the next calculation.
- Now watch the combined version. It loads a value, adds three, applies ReLU and saves the final answer. It can use the intermediate value immediately, so it doesn’t need a separate array for it.
- [Let the animation finish.]
- We get zero, four and seven in both versions. The combined version saves the work of writing and reading the temporary array.
- For a small array, that might seem minor. Across large tensors and repeated model calls, it can become a lot of data movement.
- We’re following one value at a time in the animation. On the GPU, many values can be processed in parallel.
takeaway: Both plans compute the same result; one avoids a temporary tensor.
transition: A compiler can find opportunities like this across a larger program.

title: How a compiler transforms a program
notes:
- A compiler takes a program and translates it into a form the machine can run.
- To do that, it builds a description of the program’s operations and the values each operation needs. That description is called an intermediate representation, or IR.
- [Start the compiler animation with Space.]
- The program passes through that representation on its way to instructions for the target machine. Having the operations written out makes it easier to inspect and change them.
- [Wait until the fixed expression is replaced by its result.]
- Here, the compiler already knows the inputs to a calculation. It can work out the answer while compiling and put that answer into the program. The running program then has less to do.
- A transformation like that is called an optimization pass. It has to keep the program’s required behavior intact.
- You may also hear the word lowering. That means turning a representation into one closer to what the target machine executes.
- Compilers do this for many kinds of programs. For models, they can use what they know about operations on tensors.
takeaway: A structured representation makes program transformations possible.
transition: Here’s what that looks like when we run a model.

title: Compiling tensor operations
notes:
- A model contains operations on whole arrays, such as matrix multiplication. The compiler can see how those operations connect and decide how to execute them together.
- In the top row, it prepares an execution plan. In the common torch.compile workflow, much of that preparation starts when we first call the model with actual inputs.
- That first call can be slow because it includes compilation as well as execution.
- The lower row shows later calls using the saved plan. They can take new input values and compute new answers without repeating all the preparation, as long as the plan still applies.
- This makes compilation useful for work we run repeatedly. We pay a preparation cost and hope to save enough on later calls to make it worthwhile.
- We’ll come back to measuring those costs at the end. For now, we’re focusing on inference: running a model whose weights are already trained.
takeaway: Tensor structure supports optimization, and compatible calls can reuse compiled work.
transition: Before we look at the execution plan, let’s look at where the time goes.

title: The cost of moving data
notes:
- A GPU kernel is a program launched to do work on the GPU. A model usually runs many of these programs.
- The data lives in GPU device memory. There are also smaller storage resources closer to where the calculations happen.
- [Start the memory animation with Space.]
- Watch the values being loaded into that smaller working area. Once they’re there, we’d like to get as much use from them as we can before loading more.
- [Let the animation finish.]
- For a simple calculation, fetching and storing the numbers can take more time than the arithmetic. Reducing those transfers can make a big difference.
- Other workloads spend most of their time calculating, or launching small kernels. We need to know which cost matters in the workload we’re trying to improve.
takeaway: Data movement can be a major execution cost.
transition: The compiler uses those costs to choose how the operations will run.

title: Choosing an execution plan
notes:
- This graph shows the operations and the values flowing between them.
- [Start the execution-plan animation with Space.]
- The compiler chooses how to run each part. It can use an existing library for a large operation, generate a kernel, or put several compatible operations into the same kernel.
- [Wait until the grouped plan appears.]
- So the graph and the kernels don’t need to match one for one. Several graph operations can become one kernel, and a model can use a mixture of library calls and generated code.
- The part of the compiler that targets a particular kind of hardware is called the backend. It helps turn the graph into work that hardware can execute efficiently.
- Throughout this talk, we’re keeping the model’s weights and precision fixed. We want to improve how this computation runs.
takeaway: An execution plan maps tensor operations to hardware work.
transition: Let’s look more closely at fusion, which we saw in the opening example.

title: Fusion avoids an intermediate tensor
notes:
- Here we’re adding a bias to a tensor and then applying ReLU.
- [Start the fusion animation with Space.]
- The first kernel reads the input, adds the bias and writes a temporary tensor. The next kernel reads that temporary, applies ReLU and writes the output.
- When we fuse the operations, the second calculation can use the first calculation’s result immediately. That removes the temporary tensor’s write and read.
- [Let the animation finish.]
- With a large tensor, those two transfers can involve a lot of data. Removing them is the main saving in this example.
- Fusion needs to fit the computation. If another part of the program needs that intermediate tensor, we may still have to store it. The operations also need to work together within the hardware’s resources.
- Sometimes an optimized library already includes this combination. The compiler can use that implementation too.
takeaway: Fusion can remove an intermediate store and reload.
transition: Here’s the sequence inside the fused kernel.

title: Inside the fused computation
notes:
- We read a value, add three, apply ReLU and write the result.
- The value after addition is still needed for the calculation. We just use it locally, without saving it as a separate tensor for another kernel to read.
- Keeping more values locally uses limited space on the GPU. If a fused kernel needs too much of that space, it can become slower.
- That’s one reason a compiler has to choose which operations to combine, and why we still measure the result.
takeaway: Intermediate values can stay inside the fused computation.
transition: We can count the memory accesses saved in this example.

title: Counting the removed traffic
notes:
- Assume each number takes four bytes.
- In the separate version, we read the input, write the temporary, read the temporary and write the output. That’s four accesses, or sixteen bytes per element.
- In the fused version, we read the input and write the output. That’s eight bytes per element.
- For N elements, the counts on the slide are sixteen N and eight N bytes. We’ve left bias reads out to keep this example simple.
- These counts describe the accesses in the program. Caches affect how much reaches physical memory, and execution also includes arithmetic and launch time. So we can’t turn this directly into a promised speedup.
takeaway: The example removes a temporary write and read, not half of all runtime.
transition: Now let’s look at another way to reduce reads: reusing inputs across several outputs.

title: Several outputs reuse the same inputs
notes:
- In matrix multiplication, we calculate each output using a row from the first matrix and a column from the second.
- [Start the matrix animation with Space.]
- For the first output, we multiply one by five and two by seven, then add them. Five plus fourteen gives nineteen.
- For the next output, we multiply one by six and two by eight. Six plus sixteen gives twenty-two.
- [Let the animation finish, then point to the shared row.]
- Both calculations used the same row: one and two. We can keep those values nearby and use them for the next output.
- That reuse becomes useful across large matrices, where the same input values contribute to many results.
takeaway: Several outputs need some of the same input values.
transition: Tiling organizes that reuse across blocks of the matrices.

title: Tiling reuses loaded blocks
notes:
- A tile is a block of an array. We’ll follow the highlighted block of four outputs and see how it gets calculated.
- Each output needs a row from A and a column from B. Those rows and columns extend across more values than we want to load at once, so we work through them in chunks.
- [Keep playback paused. If revisiting, click Reset animation. Press ] once to reach 4 seconds and highlight the output block.]
- This program is responsible for the two-by-two output block. It will keep four running totals, one for each output position.
- We start those totals at zero. As we work through the inputs, we’ll add each chunk’s contribution to them.
- [Press ] twice to reach 12 seconds. The first contribution is now visible.]
- We’ve loaded a two-by-two block from A and one from B. Look at the top-left output. For this first chunk, its calculation is one times one plus two times five. That gives eleven.
- Eleven is a partial sum. We haven’t used the rest of the row and column yet, so we keep that sum locally while we fetch the next inputs.
- The other three positions in our output block also get partial sums. The loaded inputs are shared across these calculations. For example, a row from the A block contributes to both output columns.
- That’s where the reuse comes from. A loaded value helps with several outputs before we replace it.
- [Press ] once to reach 17 seconds and highlight the next input blocks.]
- Now we move across A and down B to the next chunk. We keep the same output block and its running totals.
- For the top-left output, the next input pairs are three and nine, then four and thirteen. Three times nine is twenty-seven. Four times thirteen is fifty-two.
- Those contribute another seventy-nine. Adding that to the eleven already accumulated gives ninety.
- [Press ] twice to reach 28 seconds and show the completed output block.]
- The top-left output is now ninety. The same process has completed the other three outputs in the tile. We can store the finished block.
- The output grid in the animation shows the running sums so we can follow them. During the calculation, a kernel can keep these sums in local accumulators and write the final results after all the chunks are processed.
- So we’re reusing loaded inputs across outputs, and holding partial results while we move through the input chunks.
- You might now ask why we don’t make the tile much larger. More outputs could reuse the same loaded values.
- The difficulty is that every extra output needs a running total. Larger input blocks also take space. Registers and shared memory are limited.
- If one program uses too much of that space, fewer programs can run together. Values may also spill into slower memory. The extra reuse can then be outweighed by those costs.
- A very small tile has the opposite problem: it may leave useful reuse on the table and require more separate blocks of work.
- The compiler or library chooses a tile size for the matrix dimensions and the hardware. Some implementations try candidate sizes and measure them.
- The animation shows the block algorithm. Thread assignments and hardware instructions are additional choices inside the implementation.
takeaway: Loaded input blocks can contribute to several outputs before being replaced.
transition: There’s also time spent getting these kernels started. That’s the next cost we’ll look at.

title: Reusing a prepared launch sequence
notes:
- The CPU submits kernels for the GPU to run. Submitting each one takes some work.
- If the kernels are short, that repeated setup can be a noticeable part of the total time.
- [Start the replay animation with Space.]
- Look at the gaps in the upper timeline. The lower timeline uses a prepared sequence, so there’s less setup between kernels.
- [Let the animation finish.]
- CUDA Graph replay lets us prepare a sequence and submit it again with less repeated overhead. The kernels still run, using the current inputs to calculate new outputs.
- The compiler graph we saw earlier describes calculations and dependencies. A CUDA Graph records GPU work for execution and replay.
- Replay has requirements around things like memory addresses and supported operations. The runtime has to manage those requirements for it to work.
- This timeline is drawn to show the idea. In a workload with long-running kernels, these gaps may account for very little of the total time.
takeaway: Replay reduces repeated launch overhead while still executing the computation.
transition: To reuse compiled work safely, we also need to check the inputs.

title: When a saved plan can be reused
notes:
- Let’s follow several calls to a compiled model. This is an example of how reuse affects the time each request takes.
- Suppose the first input has one hundred and twenty-eight rows and two hundred and fifty-six columns. The weights, data type and device stay the same throughout this example.
- On the first call, the system captures the supported computation and prepares plan A. That call includes compilation, so it can take much longer than a warmed call.
- Before later calls use plan A, the runtime checks its assumptions. These checks are called guards.
- [Keep playback paused. If revisiting, click Reset animation. Press ] twice to reach 8 seconds and show reuse of plan A.]
- Our second call has the same shape but different numbers inside the tensor. It can use plan A again. The kernels run on the new values and calculate new outputs.
- We still do the model computation. The saving is that we don’t have to prepare the same compiled work again.
- For the third call, let’s consider a smaller shape change. Suppose plan A was compiled to support between sixty-four and one hundred and sixty rows, while keeping the column count at two hundred and fifty-six.
- That supported range is an assumption for this spoken example. A different compilation might specialize to one exact shape instead.
- Our third input has one hundred and sixty rows. It’s different from the first input, but it’s still within plan A’s supported range. If the other guards pass, this call can reuse plan A too.
- This call isn’t separately drawn in the animation. It helps explain why changing the shape doesn’t automatically mean recompiling.
- [Press ] twice to reach 16 seconds and show the request with 192 rows failing the shape check.]
- The fourth call has one hundred and ninety-two rows. That’s outside the range we assumed for plan A, so the runtime can’t use that plan for this input.
- [Press ] once to reach 20 seconds and show plan B.]
- In the path shown here, the system builds another plan. That request pays preparation time as well as execution time, so it may be noticeably slower.
- If another request arrives with the same supported shape, it may reuse plan B. The system can have several compiled variants available for different inputs.
- [Press ] once to reach the final frame at 24 seconds.]
- Other execution paths may use a more general plan that already exists, or fall back to ordinary execution. The guard check tells us the old plan doesn’t apply; it doesn’t require the same response in every situation.
- This is why a single average latency can hide important behavior. Most requests may reuse a plan quickly, while occasional requests pay for compilation.
- For a service, we’d want to test the shapes we expect and warm the relevant paths before traffic where practical. We’d also watch whether new variants keep appearing during normal use.
- So we have four calls: preparation on the first, reuse on the second, reuse for a supported shape change on the third, and another path for the unsupported shape on the fourth.
takeaway: Reuse depends on checked assumptions, not identical input values.
transition: For inputs that vary in length, there are a couple of common approaches.

title: Handling different input shapes
notes:
- Think of a voice assistant receiving recordings of different lengths.
- With dynamic shapes, we can have a program that handles a supported range of lengths. Several inputs can then use the same program.
- With bucketing, we choose a few sizes and group recordings by size. We pad a shorter recording to fit its bucket, then use the plan for that bucket.
- Padding means doing some extra computation. It can still be worthwhile if it helps us reuse a smaller set of plans.
- A dynamic program handles variation more directly, but its performance also depends on the computation and hardware.
- We compare these approaches using the lengths and batch sizes we actually expect. That tells us whether the extra preparation or padding is worthwhile.
takeaway: Shape handling is a workload-dependent execution choice.
transition: Even with a good plan, the saving depends on how much of the full run it improves.

title: A faster part may barely change the whole
notes:
- Suppose a run takes one hundred units of time. We make one half twice as fast, so that half drops from fifty to twenty-five.
- The other half still takes fifty. Together they take seventy-five, giving a twenty-five percent reduction overall.
- We also have to include the cost of compiling. If we only run the computation a few times, we may never recover that cost.
- That’s why we measure the full run as well as individual kernels.
takeaway: Measure the full workload and account for preparation cost.
transition: An LLM serving many requests gives us a useful example of repeated computation.

title: Compilation inside LLM serving
notes:
- An LLM begins by processing the prompt. That’s called prefill. It then generates tokens one step at a time, in the decode phase.
- It keeps cached attention data from earlier steps, and each new token requires more model computation.
- Because those steps repeat, small costs can add up. Fusion and data reuse can help parts of the calculation, while prepared launches can reduce submission overhead.
- A serving engine combines this compiled work with optimized kernels for operations such as attention and matrix multiplication.
- It also schedules requests and manages cached data. Those parts affect what users experience, so we measure the service under realistic traffic.
- Batch size and prompt length can change where the time goes. We want to see whether users receive tokens sooner, or whether we can serve more requests at the latency we need.
takeaway: Compilation is one execution layer within a larger serving system.
transition: The hardware matters too. Let’s connect this to custom AI chips.

title: Targeting custom AI chips: Jalapeño
notes:
- This conceptual diagram shows how model operations can reach different hardware through different software paths.
- A GPU and a custom accelerator have different instructions and memory resources. A compiler backend helps choose implementations that fit the target, together with optimized libraries and a runtime.
- The fusion and tiling ideas we’ve discussed still apply. The details change with the chip: how much data fits nearby, how it’s arranged, and which calculations the hardware can perform efficiently.
- Some mechanisms are specific to a platform. CUDA Graph replay, for example, belongs to NVIDIA’s software stack.
- [Point to the Jalapeño example.]
- OpenAI and Broadcom unveiled Jalapeño in June 2026. It’s a custom accelerator designed for LLM inference.
- OpenAI reported engineering samples running model workloads in the lab, including GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark. The announcement planned initial deployment by the end of 2026.
- That gives us a public example of a real model workload running on custom hardware. The reported stage was lab testing, with deployment still planned.
- The software has to turn the model’s operations into work that uses the chip well. That’s where hardware-specific compilation and libraries are important.
- The announcement doesn’t describe OpenAI’s internal compiler stack. We’re using the diagram to explain the general architecture, rather than claiming a particular compiler targets Jalapeño.
takeaway: Custom hardware needs software that maps model computation efficiently to its resources.
transition: You can try the same general approach on an existing PyTorch model.

title: A first compilation experiment
notes:
- Here’s a small starting point. We have a loaded model and an example input, and we keep the original model as our reference.
- We pass the model to torch.compile to get a compiled version. Its first execution can include the preparation we discussed earlier.
- The eval call sets evaluation behavior for things like dropout. Inference mode turns off gradient-tracking work that we don’t need here.
- We run both versions with the same weights and precision. That gives us outputs to compare before we start timing them.
takeaway: Try compilation on existing repeated computation while preserving a reference path.
transition: Here’s how to make that comparison useful.

title: Checking correctness and measuring runtime
notes:
- Start by comparing the outputs. Choose numerical tolerances that make sense for the model and precision. If the task has an important quality check, run that too.
- Keep the weights and precision the same in both versions so we can see the effect of compilation.
- Measure the initial call separately. Then warm up both versions and time repeated calls. Use several measurements so one unusual run doesn’t decide the result.
- There’s one detail to watch with GPUs: the CPU can finish submitting work while the GPU is still running it. A host timer may therefore stop too early.
- GPU events can measure device execution time. For wall-clock timing, synchronize at the appropriate boundaries so the interval includes the work we want to measure.
- Repeat the comparison across the input shapes you expect to use. Shape changes can affect both preparation and execution.
- If the compiled version is slower, that’s useful to know. Keep that result and investigate where the time went.
- The full agent prompt and debugging references are available through Contents.
takeaway: Check correctness, separate startup from warmed timing, and measure representative work.
transition: That brings us back to the example we started with.

title: More efficient execution of the same computation
notes:
- We got the same answer while avoiding a temporary write and read. Across a model, a compiler can look for similar savings and choose implementations for the hardware.
- You can test this on a computation you already run repeatedly. Check its outputs, measure the full run and see whether compilation helps.
takeaway: A different execution plan can preserve the computation and reduce its cost.
